teaser: The only work Michelangelo ever signed, and the story says he did it out of wounded pride.
review_notes:
Opening anecdote (visitors from Lombardy crediting the statue to a Milanese sculptor, Michelangelo carving his name at night) comes from Vasari and is told as a story, not as fact.
Signature text: MICHAEL ANGELUS BONAROTUS FLORENT FACIEBAT, on the sash across Mary's chest; letters are not legible in this photo, the spot marks the sash.
Patron: French cardinal Jean de Bilheres; contract August 1498, guarantee by banker Jacopo Galli ('most beautiful work in marble in Rome'). Cardinal died 1499.
Michelangelo's explanation of Mary's youth is reported by his biographer Condivi.
Four fingers of Mary's left hand broken in 1736 and restored: check.
1964 New York World's Fair loan; 1972 attack by Laszlo Toth (May 21), left arm broken at the elbow, nose and eyelid damaged, restoration about ten months: check details.
Dimensions 174 x 195 cm.
Tree stump under Christ's left foot: a stump-like support is visible at right in the photo; check.
Fingers broken in 1736 'during one of the statue's moves': the circumstance is uncertain, check.
Some fragments from 1972 were picked up by bystanders and some returned: check.

lesson.text: Rome, around 1500. Pilgrims crowd into a chapel beside the old St. Peter's to see a new marble group everyone is talking about. Among them, the story goes, stands the young man who carved it, unrecognized. He hears visitors from Lombardy praise it loudly. One of them explains who made it: a sculptor from Milan, of course.

The writer Giorgio Vasari, who knew Michelangelo, tells what happened next. That night the sculptor shut himself in the chapel with a lamp and his chisels, and cut his name into the stone where no one could miss it. Vasari loved a good tale, so keep a grain of salt handy. The name, however, is really there.
Where would you carve your name so that nobody could look at Mary without reading it? Tap the place.

spots.title: The sash
spots.text: A band crosses Mary's chest from shoulder to waist. Along it, in Latin capitals: “Michelangelo Buonarroti, Florentine, was making this.” It sits right over her heart.

lesson.text: He never signed anything again. Not the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, not one later statue. After this, he did not need to. The sash also names his city, Florence, a small jab at anyone who thought talent like this came from elsewhere.

Michelangelo was 23 when he signed the contract in 1498. His backer, a Roman banker, promised in writing that the result would be “the most beautiful work in marble in Rome.” It was delivered about a year later.

The client was a French cardinal who wanted a sculpture for his own tomb chapel. He asked for a pietà, Italian for “pity”: the Virgin Mary holding her dead son after the crucifixion. The subject was common in France and Germany, usually carved in wood, with a stiff, bleeding Christ lying awkwardly across his mother. In Italy it was still rare.

The awkwardness had a cause. A grown man does not fit on a seated woman's lap. Lay him across her and he sticks out on both sides like a plank. Michelangelo had one block of white Carrara marble, 174 cm tall (about 5 ft 9 in), and that problem to solve.
His solution is geometry dressed as cloth. Three lines show how the two bodies lock together.

lines.label: A pyramid
lines.text: The whole group fits inside a triangle with Mary's head at the top and a very wide base. That shape feels stable and calm, like a mountain.

lines.label: A lap like a table
lines.text: Mary's knees are set far apart under her robe. They make a broad shelf, wide enough to carry a whole body.

lines.label: The body bends
lines.text: Christ is not a plank. His head falls back, his waist sinks into her lap and his legs fold down at the knee. The line follows her body instead of crossing it.

lesson.text: Now the secret behind that shelf. Mary is a giantess. If she stood up, she would tower over her son. Her small head hides it, and so does the cloth: all those deep folds below her waist swell her lower body without your noticing. You accept the trick because the drapery looks so natural.
The Pietà feels effortless because Michelangelo broke the rules of proportion on purpose and then hid the evidence under folds of marble cloth.

There is a second liberty, and people complained about it right away. Jesus died at about 33, so his mother should be near 50. Here she looks younger than he does. Asked why, Michelangelo answered, according to his biographer Condivi, that a woman of perfect purity keeps her freshness far longer than others.

lesson.title: Grief without a cry
lesson.text: Earlier pietàs showed a mother wailing. See how little this one does, and how much it says.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Eyes lowered, mouth closed, not a tear. Her sorrow is turned inward. The smooth, unlined face is the one critics found too young.

spots.title: His face
spots.text: The head tips back over her arm, lips slightly parted. There is no agony left in it. He looks asleep, which is how the Church described this death: temporary.

spots.title: The hand that holds
spots.text: Her right hand grips him under the arm so firmly that his flesh bulges between her fingers. Yet a fold of cloth lies between her skin and his: she does not touch the sacred body directly.

spots.title: The hand that speaks
spots.text: Her left hand opens toward you, palm up. It is the only gesture in the whole group. It presents the sacrifice and seems to ask what there is left to say.

lesson.text: That open hand carries the emotion that her face holds back. It is a very Italian choice. Northern sculptors made you pity by showing wounds and tears. Michelangelo, raised on ancient Roman statues, believed beauty and stillness could move you more deeply than horror.
The speaking hand is partly a repair. Four of its fingers were broken off in 1736, during one of the statue's moves, and remade by a restorer.

Then there is the skin of the stone itself. After the chisels came files, then weeks of rubbing with pumice and abrasives until the marble took a soft shine. No other work by Michelangelo is polished this far. In later years he often left surfaces rough, even unfinished. Here, at 24, he wanted to prove he could do everything.

spots.title: The falling arm
spots.text: Christ's right arm hangs straight down, fingers loosely curled among the folds. Its dead weight tells you more plainly than any wound that life has left this body.

spots.title: Ribs and muscle
spots.text: Michelangelo had studied real corpses in a Florentine hospital. You see it in the ribcage, the stretched belly and the slack shoulder pushed up by Mary's hand.

spots.title: A landscape of cloth
spots.text: Below the body, the robe breaks into deep valleys and sharp ridges. These folds catch shadow, make the pale body stand out, and disguise how big Mary's lap really is.

spots.title: The veil
spots.text: The marble of the hood is carved so thin at its edge that it reads as soft fabric. It frames the face in shadow, like a small chapel of its own.

spots.title: Feet in the air
spots.text: The legs dangle past her lap and one foot rests on a low tree stump. Nothing here touches the ground with any force. The body seems almost weightless.

spots.title: The rock
spots.text: Mary sits on rough, cracked stone, not on a throne. It stands for Golgotha, the hill of the crucifixion, and its coarse surface makes the polish above look even finer.

lesson.text: In 1964 the Pietà crossed the Atlantic by ship, packed in a floating crate, to be shown at the New York World's Fair. Visitors glided past it on moving walkways.

On May 21, 1972, a man climbed over the altar rail and struck the statue again and again with a hammer. Mary's left arm broke off at the elbow. Her nose and an eyelid were chipped. Restorers spent months refitting the fragments, some of them returned by bystanders who had pocketed them.

Since then the Pietà has stood behind bulletproof glass, several steps back from the crowd. Those first pilgrims could lean close enough to argue over who made it. You have to read the sash from far away. But at least you know the name.

quiz.question: Where did Michelangelo carve his signature?
options: On the rock under Mary's feet
On the sash across Mary's chest
On the back of the group
quiz.explanation: The Latin inscription runs along the band that crosses her chest.

quiz.question: What does the word “pietà” refer to?
quiz.explanation: It is Italian for “pity” and names the image of the Virgin with the dead Christ on her lap.

quiz.question: How did Michelangelo make a grown man fit on Mary's lap?
options: He carved Christ as a child
He made Mary much larger and hid it under drapery
quiz.explanation: Mary is oversized, and the deep folds of her robe conceal it.

quiz.question: Why does Mary look so young, according to the explanation reported by Condivi?
options: The model was the sculptor's sister
The marble block was too small for wrinkles
quiz.explanation: Michelangelo reportedly said a perfectly pure woman keeps her youth.

quiz.question: Which gesture carries most of Mary's emotion?
quiz.explanation: Her face is still; the open, upturned left hand does the speaking.

quiz.question: What happened to the statue in 1972?
options: It was stolen for a week
It was shipped to New York
It was attacked with a hammer
quiz.explanation: A man struck it repeatedly, breaking Mary's arm and damaging her face.

facts.text: Michelangelo signed most of his sculptures.
facts.explanation: The Pietà is the only work he ever signed.

facts.text: The Pietà is the most highly polished of Michelangelo's works.
facts.explanation: He rubbed the marble for weeks; later he often left surfaces rough.

facts.text: The Pietà was carved for a French cardinal's tomb chapel.
facts.explanation: The cardinal ordered it for his own burial chapel beside old St. Peter's.
